newsitem.title: ITALY: Pope's operation starts - hospital sources.
newsitem.headline: Pope's operation starts - hospital sources.

text.p: Doctors began operating on Pope John Paul on Tuesday to remove his appendix, according to hospital sources, amid speculation that there may be more to his illness than has been revealed.

The sources said the Pope, 76, was taken into the operating theatre on the ninth floor of Rome's Gemelli hospital at around 7.15 a.m. (0515 GMT). A medical bulletin was expected to be issued at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT).
Italian newspapers openly speculate that the Pope is suffering from Parkinson's disease, a neurological disorder, and the Vatican has not specifically denied these reports.
The sources said the Polish-born Pope said prayers in the chapel of his heavily-guarded 10th floor hospital suite where early morning mass was celebrated before his operation.
It was not clear how long the surgery would last. Italian radio said the operation, by traditional incision rather than modern keyhole surgery, could take two to three hours.
The surgery was announced by the Vatican last month when it said recurrent inflammation of the appendix was the cause of three bouts of "intestinal fever" the Pope has suffered since Christmas.
The Pope, who has asked the world's 960 million Roman Catholics to pray for him, is being treated at the Gemelli by a team made up of some of Rome's leading doctors.
It is led by Professor Francesco Crucitti, the surgeon who saved the Pope's life in May 1981 after he was shot by Turkish gunman Mehmet Ali Agca in St Peter's Square.
Crucitti operated on the Pope again in 1981 and in July 1992, when a tumour the size of an orange was removed from his colon as it was starting to turn malignant.

Last month's appendix announcement has failed to quell intense speculation that the Pope may be suffering from a new tumour, a theory dismissed by the Vatican when the Pope entered the Gemelli on Sunday as "medical fiction".

It has not specifically denied reports that the Pope also has Parkinson's Disease. The neurological disorder can be marked by the sort of violent trembling that has become increasingly apparent in the Pope's left hand.
The Pontiff, who this month celebrates 18 years as leader of the world's Roman Catholics, had a battery of preparatory tests on Monday ahead of surgery.
Doctors said he was patient and calm as he underwent the examinations, including blood and urine tests, an electrocardiogram, an echo-doppler to monitor the quality of blood flow and a chest X-ray.
The chief cardiologist on the medical team, Professor Attilio Maseri, pronounced the Pope's heart completely fit.
"He's a good patient. I don't think he's very happy to be having these tests," said one senior medical source at the Gemelli hospital, where the Pontiff was admitted late on Sunday.
"No one likes to be in a hospital, would you?"
The "Pilgrim Pope" has repeatedly said he wants to lead the Catholic Church into the third millennium and has kept up a punishing schedule despite frequently appearing to be in pain.
Polish Cardinal Jozef Glemp told Vatican Radio on Monday evening he hoped the Pope "can quickly return to his mission and next year take his awaited trip to Poland".
Barring complications, the Pope is expected to stay in hospital for about five days prior to convalescence.
